name: Split-flap
basis: why: each character is a drum of flaps that clatters through every character in between; how: flip count from brightness, two-half flap animation
note: A mechanical display, filed in the device family; animated.

lumenary.blurb: An airport departures board that flips its way to your picture, then flips away.

facts.bestOn: High contrast pictures with simple shapes

why: A split-flap board has no screen: each character is a drum of flaps, and to change a letter the drum clatters through every character in between. This treatment recreates that. A cell showing a target number flips that many times, and since cells start with different delays the picture resolves as a ripple across the board.
how: Turn the picture into a grid of cells and read the brightness of each.
Pick a target position on the drum from the brightness: a ten symbol drum from blank to heavy, or letters and digits.
Flip each cell through that many flaps at 70 milliseconds a flap.
Delay each cell according to its row, column and a little random hash, so the picture appears in a diagonal wave.
Draw each flap in two halves: the top shrinks towards the hinge, then the new bottom opens out.
history: Flap displays were developed in the 1950s, and the Italian company Solari di Udine made them a fixture of railway stations and airports across the world. Their rhythm of clacking was one of the sounds of travel until LED and LCD boards replaced most of them in the 2000s and 2010s. Some are still kept for their charm.
uses: Retro station and travel themed posters
terms: The rotating spool of flaps that carries the characters.
The line along which each flap turns.
A function that gives repeatable pseudo-random numbers from inputs.
paragraphs: A real split-flap board holds a drum of characters; to show a letter, the drum flips through every character before it, one flap at a time. The program does exactly that. The picture becomes a grid of cells, and each cell’s brightness picks a target position on its drum (a ten-symbol drum running from blank to heavy, or the alphabet and digits). A cell showing target number t flips t times at a fixed 70 milliseconds a flap.

Cells do not start together. Each has a delay that grows with its column and row plus a small random amount from a coordinate hash, so the picture resolves in a diagonal ripple. After a hold, the board flips on through the rest of the drum back to blank, and the cycle repeats. A single flap is drawn in two halves: in the first half of its turn the top flap falls, shrinking vertically toward the hinge; in the second half the new bottom flap opens out. The vertical scale of a hinged card seen from the side is the cosine of its angle; the code uses a straight line from 1 to 0 to 1 as a cheap stand-in for that cosine, which looks the same at this speed.

equations.note: Target drum position of cell i on a drum of M characters.
Start delay of a cell, and the number of flaps it has completed at time τ.

equations.tex: \text{scale}=\begin{cases}1-2f&0\le f<\tfrac12\ \text{(top flap falls)}\\2f-1&\tfrac12\le f<1\ \text{(bottom flap opens)}\end{cases}\ \approx\ \lvert\cos\pi f\rvert
equations.note: Vertical scale of the moving flap during one flip, f being progress through it.

presets.text: Letters and digits make the picture spell out its tones.
More tiles give a sharper reveal.
Original colours turn it into a flipping mosaic.
